title: Simple attention
hookLine: a cook, a reformer and a poet agree: prayer can be mostly looking

cards: "Be still and see that I am God." That's the psalm, in the Douay-Rheims. Notice the verbs.
Not speak. Not ask. Not explain.
Be still, and see. Prayer often means talking, and talking is good.

But over these weeks in Carmel, a different kind has kept surfacing under the stories: the hermit's cell, Teresa's friend, John's night, Elizabeth's inner room. Strip them back, and what's left is something very plain.

teach.b: First, Teresa. In The Way of Perfection, writing to her sisters, she says she isn't asking for long reflections or clever thoughts about God. She asks only that they look at him.

If you're tired or sad, she says, look at him tired and sad in the gospel, and he will look back at you. Second, John of the Cross. When meditation dries up, John says, a person shouldn't panic and force more thinking.
They can rest in what he calls a loving attention to God, quiet and peaceful, not doing much at all. That isn't laziness, he says. It's letting God do the work.
Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection was a Carmelite lay brother in Paris who spent years in the monastery kitchen. His letters and conversations were gathered after his death.
He describes keeping himself in God's presence by a simple attention and a loving gaze, in the clatter of the kitchen just as in chapel. For him, turning an omelet could be prayer.
Fourth, what it isn't. Simple attention doesn't mean emptying the mind or forcing a feeling. It means noticing God the way you'd notice someone you love across a room: warmly, without a speech.
A reformer, a poet, a cook: three different lives, and the prayer underneath sounds the same in all three. Carmel, at its plainest, is someone looking at God with love, and letting that be enough.

how: Carmelites keep times of silent prayer each day in which they rest in loving attention to God, and some Catholics practice Brother Lawrence's habit of turning to God in the middle of ordinary work.

games.q: you've prayed with thoughts and words for years, and now they've dried up. sitting down to pray feels empty. what does John of the Cross suggest?
o: force more thinking until the feeling returns.
rest in a quiet, loving attention to God.
games.why: John says not to panic and force it, but to rest in loving attention, letting God do the work.

practice: Don't plan anything to say; just turn your attention gently toward God, the way you'd glance at someone you love who's reading in the same room. When thoughts come, and they will, don't fight them: notice, and turn back.
If you pray, let one word carry the attention, a name, or just: here; if you don't, rest your attention warmly on the breath, and stay.

wordCard.voice: Simple attention. Carmel's plainest prayer: looking at God with love, without a speech. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: loving attention. The dishes and the drive can hold it too, as the kitchen did for Brother Lawrence. Go gently.
